Here's where to start
 How much will your plan cost? Do you qualify for savings? Here's how to find out the info you need to navigate the Health Insurance Marketplace
 By Emily Brindley , Staff Writer Oct 28, 2026 Marketplace open enrollment begins on Nov. 1 and runs until Jan. 15. Within that window, there are two different deadlines.
 2022 File Photo/Tribune News Service For many people, it comes down to affordability.
 The ACA Marketplace offers a host of health insurance plans, from large companies to niche insurers and from comprehensive coverage to emergency-only safety nets.
 It’s a big world. 
 Advertisement
 Article continues below this ad
 Many folks looking for coverage on the Marketplace are either self-employed or don’t have employer-provided health coverage. But you can look for a Marketplace plan even if you do have employer-provided coverage.
 Here’s how to figure out if a Marketplace plan is a good fit for you, and how to start narrowing down your options to specific plans:
 What is the Marketplace?
 The Health Insurance Marketplace is a government-operated platform where people can purchase health coverage plans for themselves and their families, under the Affordable Care Act.
 Some states operate their own marketplaces, which are called exchanges. Other states use the federal government’s exchange.
 Advertisement
 Article continues below this ad
 Texas is among the states that use the federal exchange, which can be accessed online at HealthCare.gov .
 When is open enrollment for ACA plans?
 Marketplace open enrollment begins on Nov. 1 and runs until Jan. 15. There are two different deadlines in that window.
 Those who enroll in a plan between Nov. 1 and Dec. 15 will be covered by that plan beginning on Jan. 1.
 Those who enroll in or change plans between Dec. 16 and Jan. 15 will have coverage beginning on Feb. 1.
 Advertisement
 Article continues below this ad
 If you want to enroll in a Marketplace plan or change your coverage, open enrollment is the time to do that. But if you miss the window — or if your life circumstances change — you may qualify for a Special Enrollment Period that allows you to select or change plans during other times of the year.
 Who can enroll in a Marketplace plan?
 Typically, the people who are most likely to look for a Marketplace plan are people who are self-employed or otherwise don’t have health insurance through an employer.
 If you do have employer-provided insurance but you aren’t satisfied with those options, you can choose to enroll in a Marketplace plan. Some people who do have other insurance options, though, will find that an ACA plan would be very expensive for them. 
 On Marketplace plans, individuals and families may qualify for subsidies, which can leave the enrollee with less to pay on premiums and out-of-pocket costs.
 Advertisement
 Article continues below this ad
 Those savings are based largely on income and on family size. Individuals are likely to receive less in subsidies, for instance, than individuals in the same income bracket who also have dependents.
 People on Medicaid could sign up for Marketplace plans if they wanted to, but it would be unnecessary, and they aren’t eligible for subsidies to help pay for Marketplace plans. People on Medicare are not allowed to sign up for Marketplace plans.
 What about immigration status?
 The full list of eligibility for Marketplace plans, based on immigration status, is available on HealthCare.gov . 
 Crucially, that federal website specifies that DACA recipients are not eligible for Marketplace coverage. Some folks with other immigration statuses, including asylees and lawful permanent residents, may be eligible.
 Advertisement
 Article continues below this ad
 People who are not eligible for Marketplace plans may be able to access healthcare at community centers near them. A nationwide search tool can help you find a center near you. That search tool turns up several centers in the Dallas area, including Prism Health North Texas locations and Los Barrios Unidos Community Clinic locations.
 How do I know if I qualify for savings?
 Georvetta Kincaid, the outreach and enrollment coordinator at North Texas Area Community Health Centers, said the best way to figure out if you’re eligible for Marketplace subsidies is to apply.
 “Everyone should apply,” she said. “The only way I can tell if they’re eligible is at the end when it says that you are approved or you’re not eligible.”
 In general, people with higher incomes will receive less in subsidies and therefore have to shoulder more of the list price of a coverage plan. Conversely, people with lower incomes will typically receive more in subsidies and have a lower portion of the list price to pay themselves.
 Advertisement
 Article continues below this ad
 “Explore your options and see what you could qualify for,” said Daniel Bouton, the vice president of health and wellness at United Way of Metropolitan Dallas.
 How do I figure out how much a plan will cost?
 The federal website has a page where you can enter your state, the number of people in your household and your income bracket. That page will then allow you to preview plans with estimated prices.
 You won’t get exact details on how much you may pay until you apply.
 There are a few different aspects to any health coverage plan, and experts strongly recommend you consider all parts when selecting a plan.
 Many people look first at the monthly premium. The premium is the set amount that you will pay each month to be enrolled in a selected plan. If you qualify for subsidies, you may be responsible for only a portion of the premium each month.
 But the plan with the lowest premium may not be the cheapest for you in the long run. You should also take a look at the coverage and the deductible. 
 “We always encourage our clients to look beyond the monthly premium,” Bouton said, “and really understand what they might actually pay when they need healthcare.”
 The deductible is the amount of money you have to pay in healthcare costs before your insurance will kick in. Your monthly premium does not count toward the deductible. Preventive care — such as annual physical exams — are typically covered entirely whether you’ve met your deductible or not.
 For instance, if your deductible is $2,000, you will have to pay $2,000 in healthcare costs — not counting your monthly premiums — before your plan will begin to cover costs. Once you’ve met your deductible, you will typically only be responsible for your copay or coinsurance amount, and your plan will pay for the rest.
 Here’s what that means in practice: If you choose a plan with a low premium but a high deductible, you may actually pay more in the long run because you will have to pay the full deductible before your coverage kicks in.
 When you’re comparing Marketplace plans, then, look at both the premium and the deductible. Choose a plan that balances a premium and a deductible that best meet your expected healthcare needs — and don’t inadvertently saddle yourself with a deductible you can’t afford.
 What else should I look for in a plan?
 In addition to looking at affordability, you should also consider whether there are specific medical providers you would like to be able to see in the upcoming year.
 Medical providers may not accept certain plans, so check with your doctors or other providers and ask them if they accept a plan before you sign up for it. If you don’t check, you may end up with a plan that doesn’t allow you to see the doctors you already have, or that requires you to travel to see a provider who does accept your plan.
 “Select a plan that you will be able to utilize,” Bouton said.
 Also consider if you need vision or dental coverage. Some Marketplace plans only cover medical services, so you’ll need to filter for vision and dental if you’d like that coverage, too.
 Where can I go if I need more help?
 Bouton said when people struggle to enroll in Marketplace plans, it’s not because they don’t care about having healthcare coverage.
 “Everyone that we talk to wants to get insured,” he said. “The challenge here, that I see, is understanding the complicated system and finding the coverage that fits their circumstances.”
 If you need help figuring out your Marketplace options, there are resources available.
 United Way of Metropolitan Dallas provides free, unbiased assistance with Marketplace plans through their navigators. The best way to get in touch with them is to fill out the form on their website at unitedwaydallas.org/resources/healthcare-navigators . You can also call at 214-978-0042. Bouton said the navigators are mobile, meaning they can meet with folks in-person at a public place that’s accessible to them.
 North Texas Area Community Health Centers also provides free, unbiased assistance. You can contact them by calling 817-625-4254.
 The federal HealthCare.gov website also has a search tool to find additional navigators near you.
 Oct 28, 2026 Emily Brindley Health Reporter Emily Brindley is the health reporter at The Dallas Morning News. She covers a variety of topics, including abortion and reproductive health, in North Texas and across the state. She was previously an investigative reporter at the Fort Worth Star-Telegram . Before moving to Texas in 2021, she covered the coronavirus pandemic at the Hartford Courant in Connecticut.
